most protein complexes in budding yeast are formed by a combination of constitutively expressed and periodically expressed subunits, that the periodically expressed subunits are degraded and phosphorylated, and that the periodically expressed proteins are not randomly distributed but rather form modules that are functionally and temporally coherent.
The yeast cell cycle network consists of both periodically and continuously expressed subunits.

the analysis of the dynamic formation and disassembly of protein complexes in the yeast cell cycle.
the dynamic nature of protein complexes during cell cycle progression and the mechanisms of their regulation.
the dynamics of protein complex formation during the cell cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cell cycle control is not a static but a dynamic process.
the cell cycle control system consists of a complex network of interactions between proteins, whose activities are regulated by the cell cycle.
the yeast cell cycle is driven by the temporal assembly of protein complexes, which are controlled by both periodic and constitutive proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
most complexes consist both of constitutive and periodic components.

the majority of protein complexes are assembled from both periodically and constituitively expressed proteins and that these complexes are regulated by phosphorylation, proteolysis, and just-in-time assembly.
most cell cycle complexes are assembled from both periodically and constituitively expressed proteins, which suggests that periodic expression is a mechanism for controlling complex assembly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of periodic expression and dynamic assembly of complexes provides a powerful mechanism for regulating complex activity during the cell cycle.
